title: Spontaneous emergence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction via field-cooling-induced interface engineering in 2D ferromagnetic ternary tellurides

paper_content.abstract:
Room-temperature skyrmions in the two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnet
Fe GaTe (FGaT) hold great promise for spintronics. However, the origin of the necessary
3 2
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) within its centrosymmetric lattice remains elusive. Here,
we reveal a spontaneous DMI emergence mechanism driven by field cooling (FC) in FGaT and its
analog Fe GeTe (FGeT). We show that the commonly used FC process causes the irreversible
3 2
precipitation of FeTe layers on the FGaT surface. This FeTe /FGaT heterostructure breaks the
2 2
inversion symmetry, generating a finite interfacial DMI. This phenomenon extends to analogous
FGeT, demonstrating its universality. Notably, a threshold thickness governs effective FeTe
2
precipitation and subsequent skyrmion formation. Leveraging these findings, we developed an
optothermal technique to deterministically write single skyrmions in FGaT without FC. Our
findings provides new insights into DMI origins and skyrmion manipulation in ternary tellurides,
paving the way for advanced spintronic applications.
paper_content.introduction:
Since long-range magnetic orders were realized in atomically thin materials, including
ferromagnetism (FM, e.g., CrI and Cr Ge Te 1,2) and antiferromagnetism (AFM, e.g., FePS 3,4),
3 2 2 6 3
more and more two-dimensional (2D) magnets are being investigated by thinning down van der
Waals (vdW) magnetic materials. Plenty of new magnetic properties emerge at the 2D limit, such
as layer-dependent magnetism1,5-7, strong magnetic anisotropy2,8-10, quantum anomalous Hall
effect (QAHE)11,12 and nonlinear topological magnetic structures13-15, offering unprecedented
opportunities for miniaturized spintronic devices. Among these emerging phenomena, magnetic
skyrmions—topologically protected spin textures—have garnered intense interest due to their
potential as information carriers in ultrahigh-density memory and logic architectures15-17.

The formation and stabilization of skyrmions are strongly related to the Dzyaloshinskii-
Moriya interaction (DMI), which arises from broken inversion symmetry and induces chiral spin
textures18-20. Over an extended duration, a proper DMI for generation of skyrmions relies on
growth of chiral magnetic materials14,21 or fabrication of delicately designed heterostructures with
alternative ferromagnetic and heavy-metal films16,22, where cryogenic temperature is still
necessary for the realization of skyrmions23-25.

Recently, room-temperature skyrmions and skyrmion lattice are generated in 2D
ferromagnetic material Fe GaTe (FGaT), whose Curie transition temperature (T ) is around 350-
3 2 C
380 K, by simple field cooling (FC) at moderate temperature26-33. Such breakthrough observations
herald a transformative era in the development of vdW magnets and topological magnetic orders.
However, there persists a fundamental paradox regarding the formation of skyrmions in FGaT:
where does the DMI stem from in such a centrosymmetric crystal structure (P6 /mmc). Recent
3
studies have proposed diverse origins for DMI in FGaT, including Fe vacancies30, atomic
displacement28,29, surface oxidization34,35 and intercalation of Fe atoms32. While these studies
propose miscellaneous hypotheses regarding the origin of DMI, a unified understanding of the
dominant mechanism has yet to emerge.

Apart from the above observations, an unavoidable fact has been largely neglected. To
generate skyrmions in FGaT, thermal treatment during the FC on the sample is unavoidable, and
tellurides, especially ternary compounds, are prone to phase transitions or surface
reconstruction36,37. Therefore, in this study, we investigate the influence of the FC on DMI and
skyrmion formation in FGaTand Fe GeTe (FGeT), revealing the mechanisms of the emergent
3 2
DMI in these materials. By combining the studies of Raman spectroscopy and scanning
transmission electron microscopy (STEM), we reveal that the commonly used FC process causes
the irreversible precipitation of FeTe thin layers at the surfaces of the annealed FGaT. The resulted
2
FeTe /FGaT heterostructure is considered to be the origin of the emergent DMI due to the broken
2
inversion symmetry. Similar phenomenon has been observed in the family ferromagnetic material
FGeT as well, indicating the universality of this mechanism. Additionally, the study explores the
impact of sample thickness on FeTe precipitation and skyrmion formation, indicating FeTe
2 2
precipitation plays a crucial role in triggering the onset of DMI and stabilizing skyrmions. Based
on our new findings and to further demonstrate the application potential of FGaT in future
spintronics, we successfully write and pattern single skyrmions in FGaT by laser excitation at room
temperature and without FC process. This optothermal approach enables deterministic positioning
of individual skyrmions at predefined sites, overcoming previous limitations in skyrmion
manipulation. Our findings not only resolve the paradox of DMI emergence in nominally
symmetric vdW systems but also establish a universal pathway for engineering topological spin
textures through controlled interface engineering in these materials.

Emergence of anomalous Raman signatures in FGaT during field cooling

Pristine FGaT exhibits a vdW layered structure, crystallizing in the P6 /mmc space group, as
3
schematically illustrated in Fig. 1a. Each unit cell consists of a Fe Ga slab sandwiched between
3
two Te layers. Within the Fe Ga sublayer, Fe atoms occupy two distinct Wyckoff positions, with
3
Fe atoms positioned at the top and bottom, and Fe atoms at the center of the slab33. The process
I II
of generating stable skyrmions in FGaT through FC is illustrated in Fig. 1. In its pristine state,
FGaT exhibits a maze-like domain structure with no observable skyrmion formation, as evidenced
by the Magnetic force microscopy (MFM) image shown in Fig. 1b. This observation is consistent
with the strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) of material, which inhibits the formation
of skyrmions under zero-field conditions38. To initiate skyrmion formation, the sample was heated
to 393 K—above its T —to ensure that material entered the paramagnetic phase and was fully
C
demagnetized. Subsequently, the sample was cooled back to room temperature in the presence of
an external magnetic field (~200 Oe). Following the FC process, stable skyrmions were observed
at room temperature by MFM, as demonstrated in Fig. 1c. The skyrmions exhibit an average size
of approximately 100–200 nm, in line with previously reported values30.

A significant challenge during the FC process is the unavoidable increase in temperature,
which could potentially alter the intrinsic properties of the sample. Conventional wisdom posits
that the moderate temperature rise during field cooling exerts negligible impact on the structural
integrity of FGaT. However, the intrinsic thermal sensitivity of ternary tellurides prompts a critical
inquiry: could even mild thermal perturbations during FC trigger irreversible structural
modifications? To address this, a systematic tracking of the lattice dynamics was conducted
through the use of Raman spectroscopy. The Raman spectra, presented in Fig. 1d, reveal notable
changes before and after the FC process. The spectrum in blue corresponds to the pristine FGaT at
303 K, where a broad peak around 150 cm-1 is observed, representing the lattice vibrational modes
of FGaT39. Following FC, two sharp peaks at 121 cm-1 and 140 cm-1 appear in the Raman spectrum
(red line), indicating changes in the FGaTcrystal structure. These peaks persist after undergoing
twice zero-field cooling (ZFC) processes, suggesting irreversible crystal structural changes.
Thermal decomposition of ternary tellurides has been reported to produce Te or FeTe phases
2
under external stimuli such as heating or laser irradiation36,37,40. To identify the origin of two sharp
Raman peaks that appear after field cooling, we performed phonon spectral simulations, which
clearly attribute these peaks to FeTe precipitation. Fig. 1e and 1f show the calculated phonon
2
dispersion relations for FGaT and the orthogonal FeTe , respectively. The calculated phonon
2
modes at Γ point of Brillouin zone, along with their corresponding atomic displacement patterns
and Raman shifts are shown in Fig. S2 and Fig. S3. The corresponding Raman spectra derived
from these simulations are shown in Fig. 1d as black and gray lines for FGaT and FeTe ,
2
respectively. These theoretical spectra exhibit a high degree of correspondence with the
experimental data, suggesting that the two sharp peaks observed in the Raman spectrum are
attributable to the lattice vibrations of FeTe , with the peaks at 121 cm-1 and 140 cm-1
2
corresponding to the A and B Raman modes of FeTe 41.
g 1g 2
To further validate this hypothesis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements
were performed on FGaT samples at various temperatures. Fig. S4a and S4b show the fine spectra
of Fe 2p in XPS of FGaT at 20 and 160 °C. At 20 °C, the spectrum shows only Fe0 and Fe3+,
consistent with the pristine FGaT phase33. However, the spectrum at 160°C reveals coexistence of
Fe0, Fe2+, and Fe3+, suggesting the presence of both FGaT and FeTe phases, given that the valence
2
states of Fe in FeTe is Fe2+. As demonstrated in Fig. S4c, the proportion of Fe2+ increased
2
gradually with increasing temperature, indicating a temperature-driven precipitation of FeTe .
2
Additionally, for samples that exhibited FeTe Raman signals after annealing, a re-exfoliation
2
process was employed to remove the surface layers and Raman spectroscopy was subsequently
performed on the freshly exfoliated region. The resulting Raman spectra were found to be identical
to those observed in the pristine samples, indicating that the majority of the FeTe precipitation are
2
formed on the surface of FGaT after annealing (Fig. S5).

Surface structural reconstruction and symmetry breaking at FeTe /FGaT interface
2
Second harmonic generation (SHG) is exquisitely sensitive to the loss of inversion symmetry
in crystalline systems, making it a powerful tool for validating interfacial structural changes.To
directly probe the symmetry breaking effects induced by FeTe₂ precipitation, we performed SHG
measurements in Fig. 1g. The SHG signal is absent in pristine FGaT, which can be attributed to its
centrosymmetric crystal structure, belonging to the D point group. However, after annealing, a
6h
subtle SHG signal emerges in the FGaT sample, suggesting a symmetry-breaking effect due to the
structural changes induced by the annealing process. It is noteworthy that the orthogonal FeTe ,
2
which precipitates during the annealing process, belongs to the Pnnm space group (No. 58) and is
classified within the D point group. The crystal structure of FeTe
2h
is also centrosymmetric, and
2
thus, it would not be expected to exhibit an SHG signal. This observation implies that the SHG
signal originates from the interface between the FeTe layer and the underlying FGaT. The
2
precipitation of FeTe
2
during annealing results in an irreversible alteration of the FGaT lattice in
the heterostructure, leading to a breaking of inversion symmetry, which expectedly triggers the
onset of the DMI crucial for stabilizing topological spin textures such as skyrmions.

To further investigate the surface structural reconstruction in the annealed FGaT at atomic
scale, aberration-corrected STEM was employed to examine the crystalline structure of FGaT
nanoflakes, both before and after thermal treatment. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF)
cross-sectional STEM images of pristine FGaT along the [1 0 0] (Fig. 2a) and [1 2 0] (Fig. 2b)
directions, supported by the bright-field (BF)-STEM image (Fig. S6), reveal atomic lattice without
defects. The crystal structure reveals a Fe Ga slab is intercalated between two tellurium layers,
3
with a vdW gap separating adjacent Te atoms. No intercalation of iron atoms within the vdW gap
is observed. To mitigate ion beam damage during focused ion beam (FIB) sample preparation, a
protective graphene capping layer was applied to the surface layer of FGaT (Fig. S7). The pristine
edge structure of FGaTslab, as shown in the large-area ADF-STEM and BF-STEM images (Fig.
2c, 2d, Fig. S8), remains unchanged, preserving its pristine atomic arrangement.

Upon annealing at 220 °C, atomic rearrangements occur at both the edges of FGaT slab,
resulting in the formation of distinct non-layered structures. These changes are evidenced by the
appearance of additional diffraction spots in the fast Fourier transform (FFT) patterns that do not
correspond to FGaT (Fig. 2e, 2f). The ADF-STEM image in Fig. 2g highlights a vdW gap between
the newly formed non-layered structure and the FGaT layers, similar to the original vdW gap
observed within the FGaT sublayers. To identify the annealed structure, the atomic arrangement
of the non-layered phase was systematically examined along the [1 0 0] and [1 2 0] directions of
FGaT. As shown in Fig. 2h, the ADF-STEM image reveals orthogonal FeTe (Pnnm) along the [0
2
0 1] zone axis, with the lattice spacing of the (2 0 0) plane measured to be 1.97 Å, as confirmed
by the corresponding FFT pattern (Fig. 2i), in excellent agreement with the atomic structure model.
Further analysis of large-scale ADF-STEM images of FeTe
2
reveals diffraction spots (green
square) along the (1 1 3) plane, corresponding to [3 0 1] zone axis (Fig. S9a-9c). The atomic
arrangements along the [3 0 1] direction show a lack of alternating undulations in the tellurium
atoms, unlike those observed along the [0 0 1] direction (Fig. S9d, S9e), as demonstrated by the
detailed ADF-STEM images and FFT patterns of FeTe (Fig. S10). Additionally, the ADF-STEM
2
image along the [1 0 0] direction of FGaT and its FFT pattern confirm that FeTe exists along both
2
the [1 0 0] and [1 0 1] zone axes (Fig. 2j, 2k, Fig. S11). Given the overlapping FFT patterns and
similar atomic structure (Fig. S11), we propose that FeTe forms along both the [1 0 0] and [1 0 1]
2
directions, influenced by the biaxial orientation of FeTe along the [1 2 0] direction of FGaT. The
2
precipitation of FeTe with different crystallographic orientation can be attributed to the thermal
2
annealing process, which represents a non-equilibrium thermodynamic transformation. To verify
the elemental composition of the annealed FGaT, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
was employed, revealing a uniform distribution of Te, Fe, and Ga in the lower region of FGaT (Fig.
2l–2o). Notably, the edge region (area 1) exhibits a significant Te enrichment, with the
corresponding EDS spectra (Fig. 2p) showing an atomic ratio of Fe: Te: Ga = 1: 1.9: 0.28, closely
matching the stoichiometry of FeTe , in perfect agreement with the structural analysis.
2
Furthermore, EDS mapping of area 2 indicates diffusion of Fe atoms into the upper FeTe layer,
2
as reflected in the spectra (Fig. S12), which suggest the formation of an amorphous phase with an
Fe: Te: Ga ratio of 1: 0.19: 0.02. These findings confirm the precipitation of FeTe at the surfaces
2
of FGaT, establishing the FGaT/FeTe
2
heterostructure.

Micromagnetic simulations intuitively validate the interface-induced DMI and its impact on
topological spin textures (Fig. S13 and Fig.S14). For pristine FGaT (D = 0.1 mJ/m2, set to match
centrosymmetric constraints), field-dependent simulations reproduce only maze-like magnetic
domains, aligning with our previous experimental observations42. Conversely, the FeTe
2
/FGaT
interface (D = 2.0 mJ/m2) generates diverse spin textures, including skyrmions, bi-skyrmioniums,
and skyrmion bags which are directly attributable to interfacial DMI. Crucially, simulations
replicate the FC process: Initial maze-like domains (Fig. S14a) transform into skyrmion lattices
after FC under a 300 Oe magnetic field (Fig. S14b), mirroring experimental MFM results (Fig. 1c-
d). These simulation confirm that FeTe /FGaT interface induced DMI emergence fundamentally
2
reconfigures spin textures.

To rule out the possibility that the observed magnetic changes stem from bulk structural
modifications, we performed X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements. Large scale bulk structural
modification, specifically the self-intercalation of surplus Fe into the van der Waals gaps, is known
to sensitively alter the c-axis lattice parameter43,44. As shown in Fig. S24, the (00l) diffraction peaks
of the FGaT matrix remain sharp and maintain their positions after annealing. Quantitative analysis
reveals that the interplanar spacing remains virtually unchanged (d ≈ 0.85 Å), with a negligible
variation of ~ 0.007 Å. This stability contrasts with the significant lattice distortions (typically >
0.25 Å) observed in self-intercalated phases44, confirming that the bulk crystal structure is well-
preserved. Consequently, the symmetry breaking and emergent DMI are attributed to the
engineered interface rather than bulk intercalation effects.

Universal FeTe precipitation and interface-driven spin texture evolution in FGeT
2
The spontaneous precipitation of FeTe through thermal annealing is not merely a
2
phenomenon isolated to FGaT but represents a universal mechanism within the family of ternary
telluride, attributable to the low bond energy of the compounds. Recent studies have shown that
FGeT, a well-known family member of FGaT, undergoes thermal decomposition upon annealing,
resulting in the precipitation of FeTe and Fe Ge phases through a temperature-induced self-
2 3
decomposition mechanism37. As with FGaT, FeTe
2
precipitation exerts a comparable effect on
FGeT, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The Raman spectrum of pristine FGeT before annealing (Fig. 3a)
exhibits a broad peak near 150 cm-1, which is attributed to the characteristic peak of FGeT, as
previously reported45. Upon annealing, the Raman spectrum of FGeT displays two sharp peaks,
consistent with the results observed in FGaT. These sharp peaks correspond to the characteristic
vibrations of FeTe , indicating that the precipitation of FeTe also occurs in FGeT after thermal
2 2
treatment.

To further investigate the atomic structure and chemical composition of the annealed FGeT,
graphene-capped cross-sectional ADF-STEM imaging and EDS analysis were conducted (Fig.
S15). The pristine cross-sectional FGeT nanosheet exhibits the similar atomic arrangement as
FGaT (Fig. S16) , and the EDS mapping shows a uniform distribution of Fe, Ge, and Te, with an
atomic ratio of Fe: Ge: Te = 3: 1: 2 (Fig. S17). Large-scale ADF-STEM images (Fig. 3b) and their
corresponding FFT pattern (Fig. 3c) confirm the precipitation of FeTe in FGeT following the
2
same annealing process used for FGaT. Detailed ADF-STEM image reveals the interface between
the non-layered FeTe and the FGeT layers (Fig. 3d), which is absent in pristine FGeT (Fig. S18).
2
The thermally annealed FGeT exhibits greater sensitivity to temperature, as evidenced by the
more extensive precipitation of FeTe , with a thickness of up to 10.2 nm (Fig. S19). Moreover, a
2
clearer ADF-STEM image (Fig. 3e) of a distorted hexagonal-shaped FeTe along the [1 0 0] and
2
[1 0 1] directions shows distinct high-contrast (brighter) and low-contrast (darker) spots,
representing Te and Fe atom columns, respectively. The FFT pattern (Fig. 3f) further supports this
interpretation. The lattice arrangement of FeTe along the [1 0 0] direction shows Fe atoms
2
alternating between two adjacent tellurium layers, as confirmed by the intensity line profile (Fig.
3g). However, along the [1 0 1] direction, the Fe atoms are doubly occupied between the tellurium
layers (Fig. 3h), with the periodic intensity variation of Fe atoms resulting from the simultaneous
presence of both [1 0 1] and [1 0 0] directions in the FeTe structure. The ADF-STEM image of
2
FeTe along the [0 0 1] direction (Fig. 3i) reveals alternating undulations of Te atoms, which are
2
corroborated by the absence of characteristic diffraction spots from the [3 0 1] FeTe structure in
2
the corresponding FFT pattern (Fig. 3j).

Additionally, the precipitation of FeTe has been shown to be associated with the formation
2
of skyrmions, as observed through MFM measurements. Fig. S20 and S21 illustrate the formation
of skyrmions under an external magnetic field, both before and after annealing. In pristine FGeT,
only a few isolated skyrmions are observed in the MFM image (Fig. 3k) taken at 150 K under a
0.7 kOe magnetic field. In contrast, highly-densed skyrmion lattice formed in the annealed FGeT,
as evidenced by the MFM image (Fig. 3l) (150 K and 0.7 kOe). This transformation is attributed
to the precipitation of FeTe during the annealing process and resulting FeTe /FGeT
2 2
heterostructure, analogous to the FeTe /FGaT heterostructure, breaks the inversion symmetry and
2
gives rise to a finite interfacial DMI.

Thickness-dependent FeTe precipitation and correlated topological magnetic states
2
The ability to manipulate skyrmion properties, such as size, density, and thermal stability, is
pivotal for their integration into high-density memory and logic devices. However, achieving such
control requires a fundamental understanding of how material parameters, particularly thickness,
influence the underlying mechanisms of skyrmion formation. It has been demonstrated in recent
studies that FGaT with varying thicknesses exhibit distinct skyrmions properties, including size
and order26,30,31. Interestingly, the extant literatures appear to exhibit a thickness limit for
observable skyrmions. The critical thickness limit for the formation of skyrmions may be based
on this FeTe /FGaT heterostructure strategy, as illustrated in Fig. 4. Fig. 4 investigates the
2
temperature dependence of Raman spectra in FGaT with varying thicknesses and threshold for the
precipitation of FeTe . Fig. 4a and 4b display the temperature-dependent Raman spectra for 15 nm
2
and 70 nm thick FGaT samples, respectively. At room temperature (303 K), both samples exhibit
a broad peak around 150 cm-1, characteristic of FGaT, confirming the presence of pure FGaT
before thermal annealing. As the temperature increases, the thicker sample (70 nm) begins to
precipitate FeTe evidenced by a weak signal of A mode (~120 cm-1) of FeTe emerging at 338 K.
2 g 2
By 368 K, the two characteristic FeTe peaks are clearly visible, indicating substantial precipitation.
2
In contrast, the thinner sample (15 nm) shows subtle signal of FeTe peaks only at 373 K, with
2
more pronounced features appearing only at 423 K (Fig. S22). The two samples, differing in
thickness, exhibit a notable disparity in the temperature at which FeTe
2
precipitation occurs.

To further explore the role of thickness and temperature on FeTe precipitation, Raman
2
spectra were collected for samples with thicknesses ranging from 15 to 600 nm. As shown in Fig.
4c, FeTe precipitation exhibits a strong dependence on sample thickness. The transition
2
temperature was defined as the point at which the intensity ratio of FeTe to FGaT Raman peaks
2
exceeds 1/3 (Fig. S22), indicating a certain amount of FeTe precipitation at this temperature. This
2
approach ensures consistent quantification of FeTe
2
precipitation onset across thickness-dependent
datasets. The transition temperature reveals a distinct threshold at approximately 25 nm. For
samples thinner than 25 nm (red dots), the transition temperature ranges from 380–400 K, whereas
thicker samples (orange dots) precipitate FeTe at lower transition temperatures, between 320–350
2
K. This threshold indicates that thicker FGaT samples are more prone to FeTe
2
precipitation, with
a clear distinction in the transition temperatures based on the sample thickness. Furthermore, the
intensity ratio of FeTe to FGaT Raman peaks at the highest temperature (423 K) reinforces this
2
threshold. As shown in Fig. S22b, the ratios for thinner samples range from 1.5 to 2, while for
thicker samples, the ratios increase to 3.5 to 6. This suggests that thinner FGaT samples are less
likely to precipitate FeTe .
2
A comparison with the previous literatures (Fig. 4d) suggests that the observed thickness
threshold for FeTe precipitation closely aligns with the minimum thickness required for skyrmion
2
formation in FGaT, as reported earlier26,30. This further implies that FeTe precipitation plays a
2
critical role in skyrmion formation by providing the necessary symmetry breaking to stabilize
skyrmion lattices.

Optothermal creation of isolated single skyrmions via local phase engineering
The established link between FeTe precipitation and skyrmion stabilization was further
2
developed through the implementation of a laser annealing protocol on FGaT flake, thereby
facilitating the creation of site-specific skyrmions, which are crucial for spintronic applications.
As illustrated schematically in Fig. 5a, the FGaT sample was positioned under an out-of-plane
magnetic field with approximately 200 Oe, aligned with the FC condition. A 532 nm continuous-
wave laser was irradiated in a pre-designed 3×3 array pattern, generating localized thermal
annealing zones while maintaining an inter-spot distance of approximately 5 μm. The laser power
was set to 2.5 mW, which was optimized to be within the safe operating window for FeTe
2
precipitation (see Methods), and the irradiation time for each spot was five minutes. This duration
is sufficient to reach the temperature to induce FeTe precipitation, yet it remains well below the
2
threshold required to cause the degradation of the FGaT. This spatially selective laser annealing
process directly induced the formation of FeTe
2
nanodomains, as confirmed by Raman
spectroscopy. The Raman mapping of characteristic A
g
phonon mode at 121 cm-1 (Fig. 5b)
demonstrates exclusive intensity enhancement at all nine irradiated sites, while exhibiting no
detectable peak at this position in non-annealed regions. This site-specific spectral fingerprint
conclusively demonstrates FeTe
2
formation exclusively within laser-defined zones, with the
surrounding matrix retaining pristine FGaT characteristics. Notably, MFM image of these specific
locations revealed the presence of isolated single skyrmions, which exhibited precise positional
correspondence with the laser-defined sites. Fig. 5c shows a magnetic landscape divided by the
Raman mapping boundary (dashed box). Maze-like domains dominate the unmapped regions and
correspond to predominant ferromagnetic domains. In contrast, the scanned territory exhibits laser-
modified labyrinth-like domains, indicative of the reduced ferromagnetic phase42. Critically, only
the nine sites that were intentionally irradiated and coincided with Raman mapping hotspots
nucleated isolated single skyrmions (with diameters of 300-400 nm) that were confined to laser-
spot dimensions, demonstrating phase-specific magnetic engineering by laser control. These laser-
patterned single-skyrmion arrays enable a room-temperature operation without FC process. Their
deterministic positioning and ambient operational stability overcome persistent scalability barriers
in topological computing architectures. This breakthrough paves the way for implementing energy-
efficient spintronic logic gates with nanoscale resolution, enabling next-generation spintronic
memory and logic devices29,46. Fig. 5d demonstrates a skyrmion-based AND logic gate enabled by
our laser-directed single-skyrmion writing technique, which provides the critical foundation for
programmable topological computing. By leveraging deterministic laser patterning (Fig. 5a-c), we
successfully created individual single-skyrmion in FGaT by laser FC. Binary inputs are encoded
via single-skyrmions core polarization (up/down) defined as logic states “0” for up and “1” for
down with the polarization direction set by external magnetic field orientation during laser FC. As
illustrated in Fig. 5d, the two input skyrmions are created at the top- and bottom-right corners. A
pulse current is utilized to concurrently drive the skyrmions towards the center47,48. Input pairs
aligned in parallel (0–0 or 1–1) undergo coherent merging, preserving the topological
configuration. In contrast, antiparallel input combinations (0–1 or 1–0) result in topological
annihilation, collapsing into a trivial ferromagnetic state. The output is detected via a tunneling
magnetoresistance (TMR) sensor, which registers a logical '1' only detecting a surviving down-
polarized skyrmion. This mechanism enables Boolean AND functionality with zero static power
consumption, showcasing the feasibility of energy-efficient, reconfigurable topological logic
operations.

single crystal growth
FGaTcrystals were grown using the self-flux method. Highly pure Fe (99.9 %), Ga (99.99 %),
and Te (99.99 %) powders, with a mole ratio of 1:1:2, were mixed under Ar atmosphere in a glove box
and sealed in a quartz tube under 1.9 Pa. To capture the excess flux during centrifugation, a crucible
filled with quartz wool was placed on top of the growth crucible. The melt was homogenized at 1000 °C
for approximately 24 hours, then cooled quickly to 880 °C in 1 hour, followed by slow cooling to
780 °C in 100 hours. At this temperature, the ampoules were removed from the furnace and placed in
a centrifuge to expel the excess flux. Then large single crystals could be obtained. FGaTnanoflakes
were mechanically exfoliated onto a freshly cleaned SiO2/Si substrate
. In our experiment, the pristine
FGaT nanoflakes were mechanically exfoliated onto a freshly cleaned SiO2/Si substrate with the
thicknesses ranging from 12 to 600 nm (Fig. S1).

Magnetic force microscopy measurements
MFM measurements on FGaT were performed using the DIMENSION ICON (Bruker). The
magnetic field during FC was generated by a neodymium magnet. The measurement was conducted in
a glove box protected by high-purity nitrogen gas at room temperature. The magnetic tip from
Nanoworld coated with Co/Cr was used for all measurements. The force constant and resonance
frequency of this tip are 3 N/m and 75 kHz, respectively. During the measurement, the topography of
the sample was first acquired in tapping mode. During the second scan, the MFM tip was lifted by 100
nm above the sample to measure the magnetic signal in tapping mode. MFM measurements on FGeT
were carried out using variable temperature MFM system (attocube-2100). Hard magnetic point probes
with cobalt coating (Nanosensors) were employed. The samples were cooled from room temperature
to 150 K in a low-pressure helium gas environment under zero magnetic field. Prior to MFM imaging,
a relatively flat region was identified using tapping mode AFM, and slope compensation was
performed to ensure a constant tip-sample distance across the scan area. Phase images were then
acquired at a fixed tip-sample separation, typically set to 100 nm.

Raman Spectroscopy measurements
The Raman measurements were obtained by a Witec Alpha 300R confocal Raman microscope.
The 532 nm linear polarized laser was focused perpendicular to the surface of the sample through a
100x objective lens (numerical aperture = 0.9). The maximum power is kept below 0.2 mW to avoid
the laser thermal effects on the sample. The Raman signals were first collected by a photonic crystal
fiber and then coupled into the spectrometer with 1800 g/mm grating.

HAADF-STEM
STEM specimens were prepared by the focused ion beam (FIB) lift-out technique using the FEI
Helios 5cx system. Atomic resolution STEM images were performed on an aberration-corrected FEI
Themis Z transmission electron microscopy, equipped with a cold field-emission gun operating at 200
kV. The resolution ADF-STEM images were collected with a convergence semiangle of 24.5 mrad,
collecting scattering from >44 mrad. Image filtered using Gaussian functions.

Theoretical calculation
The relaxed crystal structures were obtained using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package
(VASP) within the framework of density functional theory (DFT). The exchange-correlation
functional was described using the general gradient approximation (GGA) as parameterized
by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE). The plane -wave energy cutoff and convergence threshold
were set to 450 eV and 10- 6 eV, respectively. Phonon spectra with a 2×2×2 supercell were

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The article describes the origin and applications of skyrmions in the 2D ferromagnetic material Fe3GaTe2 at room temperature. The authors demonstrated a spontaneous formation of FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface during field cooling, which had been overlooked in previous studies. This interface enhances the DMI which is crucial for skyrmion formation and resolves a longstanding issue of the DMI origin in Fe3GaTe2. They further demonstrated the precise generation of single skyrmions via laser-based field cooling. I believe this paper holds significant novelty and importance in both experimental mechanisms and application potential, making it worthy of publication in Nature Communications. However, there are some minor concerns.
1. The experimental evidence linking the FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface to skyrmions formation is convincing, while the theoretical explain seems a bit sparse. Can you explain more how the FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface affect the DMI enhancement?
2. SHG is important for studying symmetry. Have you tested angle-resolved polarized SHG? What should the polarization of the FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface be?
3. The article mentions the universality of FeTe2 precipitation, which might be crucial for surface structures and physics besides DMI and skyrmions. Does this phenomenon occur in other ternary tellurides?
4. The localized single skyrmions are groundbreaking. The device concept is also intriguing and promising. However, some important articles in this field have not been cited, such as (1) Nature Nanotechnology 16, 1086-1091 (2021) (2) Nature Nanotechnology 12, 123-126 (2017).
5. There are some grammatical and spelling errors. On page 2, line 21, ‘the discovery provide new insights’ should be ‘the discovery provides new insights’; On page 6, line 11, ‘valance states’ should be ‘valence states’.
After addressing these concerns, I think this article can be published in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This study focuses on the mechanism of spontaneous enhancement of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in two-dimensional van der Waals ferromagnets Fe₃GaTe₂ (FGaT) and its analog Fe₃GeTe₂ (FGeT). Above-room-temperature chiral skyrmion lattice and Dzyaloshinskii Moriya interaction in a van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3−xGaTe2 has been reported [Nat. Commun. 15, 4472 (2024)], where the DMI arises from the off-centered FeΙΙ atoms which break the spatial inversion symmetry. It has been also reported that Néel-type skyrmion in WTe2/Fe3GeTe2 van der Waals heterostructure [Nat. Commun. 11, 3860 (2020)]. Here, the authors claim that the inversion asymmetry arising from the irreversible precipitation of FeTe2 at the surface causing the DMI in FGaT(FGeT) system. Obviously, the two reported DMIs are originating from different mechanism even though in the very similar system. The research features a clear logical framework and detailed arguments. Experimentally, multiple characterization methods are employed to verify the viewpoint. The data integrity and logical consistency are reasonable, and the study has high academic value and application potential.
However, there is still room for improvement. It is recommended that the authors revise the manuscript according to the following suggestions, after which consideration may be given to accepting it for publication:
Comment-1: The article indicates that the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Interaction (DMI) strength D at the FeTe2/FGaT interface is 2.0 mJ/m2, yet it fails to provide relevant verification for this value. It is suggested to conduct additional experimental and theoretical work to further validate the DMI strength.
Comment-2: The authors have done first-principles calculations for the FGT to verify their experimental results. In page 9, the authors claim that “These computations confirm that FeTe2/FGaT interface induced DMI enhancement fundamentally reconfigures spin textures.” However, they did not give any DMI data from first-principles. I suggest the authors to do first-principles calculations for the DMI strength, following the method Phys. Rev. Lett.115, 267210 (2015); Nat. Rev. Phys. 5, 43 (2023).
Comment-3: It is suggested to add labels for temperature and magnetic field strength to Fig. 1b and Fig. 1c.
Comment-4: The article mentions that the characteristic Raman peaks of FeTe2 still exist under zero field condition, yet relevant data are lacking.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript by Xia .et.al. deals with the determination of different phases during the annealing process of Fe3GaTe2 and Fe3GeTe2 crystals and its impact on the formation of magnetic textures. The authors provide an extensive characterization to support their claims. While the data clearly points to the formation of a secondary phase (FeTe2) that precipitates in a crystalline way towards the surface, the mechanism of skyrmion formation and claimed “enhancement of DMI interaction” is not well described and understood. In particular, the occurrence of symmetry breaking and induced skyrmion-like magnetic textures can have various origins besides the claimed FGaT/FeTe2 interface , such as self-intercalation, point defects, other magnetic phases, etc. Especially in systems that undergo precipitation, a plethora of changes may occur to the initial crystal phase. It is now well known in the community that TEM data (in which the authors base) is extremely local for a crystal that is macroscopic and not necessarily representative of the sample behaviour. Additional large-scale techniques to rule out the presence of point defects (e.g. Te-deficiency) and self-intercalation of surplus Fe -which can migrate not only to the top, but also to the bottom FGaT layer,- should be employed: for instance X-ray diffraction to resolve the FGaT structure before and after annealing (akin Phys. Rev. Materials 4, 074008 (2020) and Physical Review Letters 133 (25), 256702 (2024)). Additionally, the authors should discuss the influence of second Fe-Ga precipitate phase on the magnetic properties, in particular on the effect on MFM imaging as this phase is concentrated at the surface. This is necessary to unveil the origin of the observed SHG response and skyrmion-like bubble formation which is one of the most important aspects of the paper. The authors should address this main issue in a revised manuscript, as well as several other points:
1) The Raman-signal in Figure 1 show a full transition from one phase to another, without overlap of the two phases (as it was detected by TEM, Figure 2). The authors should comment if the surface sensitivity of their Raman setup is in line with the observation of only the FeTe2 phase after annealing.
2) SHG measurements. If the creation of a non-centrosymmetric structure happens only at the interface, it might reflect on a very weak signal. However, if it comes from a rather bulk phenomenon, it should scale with thickness. The authors should perform thickness dependent SHG measurements (samples shown in Figure 4c) to corroborate the origin of the signal.
3) There is another surface layer which consists of Fe-Ga rich amorphous phase. What is the thickness and influence of this layer on the various measurements? Since it contains Fe, it is probably magnetic. Could you provide magnetization measurements of the crystals before and after annealing? Is this also possible affecting magnetic bubble formation? MFM is surface sensitive so it will actually get stronger signals from the topmost layer.
4) How do you get the DMI constant of the FeTe2/FGaT interface as D = 2.0 mJ/m2? Can you provide calculation/estimation details?
5) The title states: “enhancement of DMI”, but there is no direct experimental evidence of DMI enhancement. The magnetic bubble formation is a hint that DMI might be the reason behind, but is very qualitative and does not merit the claim in the title. Even though, it is not clear whether it is a bulk or an interface-driven DMI. Either the authors bring more quantitative evidence or they should tone down the DMI statements in the manuscript.
6) In the laser-patterning experiment, is it possible to control laser parameters and define the boundaries of FeTe2 formation, similar to the heating study? That would serve as a practical guide for other scientists that may want to reproduce the results.
7) “The bond-free vdW interfaces in FeTe2/FGaT enable seamless integration of dissimilar materials without lattice-matching constraints, preserving spin coherence for low-1 power spintronic devices.” This sentence is misleading. The preservation of spin coherence is not automatically given at a vdW interface of dissimilar materials.

## Abstract

Room-temperature skyrmions in the two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnet
Fe GaTe (FGaT) hold great promise for spintronics. However, the origin of the necessary
3 2
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) within its centrosymmetric lattice remains elusive. Here,
we reveal a spontaneous DMI emergence mechanism driven by field cooling (FC) in FGaT and its
analog Fe GeTe (FGeT). We show that the commonly used FC process causes the irreversible
3 2
precipitation of FeTe layers on the FGaT surface. This FeTe /FGaT heterostructure breaks the
2 2
inversion symmetry, generating a finite interfacial DMI. This phenomenon extends to analogous
FGeT, demonstrating its universality. Notably, a threshold thickness governs effective FeTe
2
precipitation and subsequent skyrmion formation. Leveraging these findings, we developed an
optothermal technique to deterministically write single skyrmions in FGaT without FC. Our
findings provides new insights into DMI origins and skyrmion manipulation in ternary tellurides,
paving the way for advanced spintronic applications.

---

## Introduction

Since long-range magnetic orders were realized in atomically thin materials, including
ferromagnetism (FM, e.g., CrI and Cr Ge Te 1,2) and antiferromagnetism (AFM, e.g., FePS 3,4),
3 2 2 6 3
more and more two-dimensional (2D) magnets are being investigated by thinning down van der
Waals (vdW) magnetic materials. Plenty of new magnetic properties emerge at the 2D limit, such
as layer-dependent magnetism1,5-7, strong magnetic anisotropy2,8-10, quantum anomalous Hall
effect (QAHE)11,12 and nonlinear topological magnetic structures13-15, offering unprecedented
opportunities for miniaturized spintronic devices. Among these emerging phenomena, magnetic
skyrmions—topologically protected spin textures—have garnered intense interest due to their
potential as information carriers in ultrahigh-density memory and logic architectures15-17.

The formation and stabilization of skyrmions are strongly related to the Dzyaloshinskii-
Moriya interaction (DMI), which arises from broken inversion symmetry and induces chiral spin
textures18-20. Over an extended duration, a proper DMI for generation of skyrmions relies on
growth of chiral magnetic materials14,21 or fabrication of delicately designed heterostructures with
alternative ferromagnetic and heavy-metal films16,22, where cryogenic temperature is still
necessary for the realization of skyrmions23-25.

Recently, room-temperature skyrmions and skyrmion lattice are generated in 2D
ferromagnetic material Fe GaTe (FGaT), whose Curie transition temperature (T ) is around 350-
3 2 C
380 K, by simple field cooling (FC) at moderate temperature26-33. Such breakthrough observations
herald a transformative era in the development of vdW magnets and topological magnetic orders.
However, there persists a fundamental paradox regarding the formation of skyrmions in FGaT:
where does the DMI stem from in such a centrosymmetric crystal structure (P6 /mmc). Recent
3

dominant mechanism has yet to emerge.

Apart from the above observations, an unavoidable fact has been largely neglected. To

Pristine FGaT exhibits a vdW layered structure, crystallizing in the P6 /mmc space group, as
3

3

3

of the non-layered phase was systematically examined along the [1 0 0] and [1 2 0] directions of
FGaT. As shown in Fig. 2h, the ADF-STEM image reveals orthogonal FeTe (Pnnm) along the [0
2
0 1] zone axis, with the lattice spacing of the (2 0 0) plane measured to be 1.97 Å, as confirmed
by the corresponding FFT pattern (Fig. 2i), in excellent agreement with the atomic structure model.

2
reveals diffraction spots (green
square) along the (1 1 3) plane, corresponding to [3 0 1] zone axis (Fig. S9a-9c). The atomic

2
image along the [1 0 0] direction of FGaT and its FFT pattern confirm that FeTe exists along both
2
the [1 0 0] and [1 0 1] zone axes (Fig. 2j, 2k, Fig. S11). Given the overlapping FFT patterns and

2

2

2

2

/FGaT

2
reconfigures spin textures.

variation of ~ 0.007 Å. This stability contrasts with the significant lattice distortions (typically >
0.25 Å) observed in self-intercalated phases44, confirming that the bulk crystal structure is well-
preserved. Consequently, the symmetry breaking and emergent DMI are attributed to the
engineered interface rather than bulk intercalation effects.

2
The spontaneous precipitation of FeTe through thermal annealing is not merely a
2
phenomenon isolated to FGaT but represents a universal mechanism within the family of ternary
telluride, attributable to the low bond energy of the compounds. Recent studies have shown that
FGeT, a well-known family member of FGaT, undergoes thermal decomposition upon annealing,
resulting in the precipitation of FeTe and Fe Ge phases through a temperature-induced self-
2 3
decomposition mechanism37. As with FGaT, FeTe
2

FGeT, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The Raman spectrum of pristine FGeT before annealing (Fig. 3a)

vibrations of FeTe , indicating that the precipitation of FeTe also occurs in FGeT after thermal
2 2
treatment.

2

the non-layered FeTe and the FGeT layers (Fig. 3d), which is absent in pristine FGeT (Fig. S18).
2
The thermally annealed FGeT exhibits greater sensitivity to temperature, as evidenced by the
more extensive precipitation of FeTe , with a thickness of up to 10.2 nm (Fig. S19). Moreover, a
2

2

representing Te and Fe atom columns, respectively. The FFT pattern (Fig. 3f) further supports this
interpretation. The lattice arrangement of FeTe along the [1 0 0] direction shows Fe atoms
2
alternating between two adjacent tellurium layers, as confirmed by the intensity line profile (Fig.

layers (Fig. 3h), with the periodic intensity variation of Fe atoms resulting from the simultaneous
presence of both [1 0 1] and [1 0 0] directions in the FeTe structure. The ADF-STEM image of
2
FeTe along the [0 0 1] direction (Fig. 3i) reveals alternating undulations of Te atoms, which are
2
corroborated by the absence of characteristic diffraction spots from the [3 0 1] FeTe structure in
2
the corresponding FFT pattern (Fig. 3j).

Additionally, the precipitation of FeTe has been shown to be associated with the formation
2
of skyrmions, as observed through MFM measurements. Fig. S20 and S21 illustrate the formation
of skyrmions under an external magnetic field, both before and after annealing. In pristine FGeT,
only a few isolated skyrmions are observed in the MFM image (Fig. 3k) taken at 150 K under a
0.7 kOe magnetic field. In contrast, highly-densed skyrmion lattice formed in the annealed FGeT,
as evidenced by the MFM image (Fig. 3l) (150 K and 0.7 kOe). This transformation is attributed
to the precipitation of FeTe during the annealing process and resulting FeTe /FGeT
2 2
heterostructure, analogous to the FeTe /FGaT heterostructure, breaks the inversion symmetry and
2
gives rise to a finite interfacial DMI.

Thickness-dependent FeTe precipitation and correlated topological magnetic states
2
The ability to manipulate skyrmion properties, such as size, density, and thermal stability, is
pivotal for their integration into high-density memory and logic devices. However, achieving such
control requires a fundamental understanding of how material parameters, particularly thickness,
influence the underlying mechanisms of skyrmion formation. It has been demonstrated in recent
studies that FGaT with varying thicknesses exhibit distinct skyrmions properties, including size
and order26,30,31. Interestingly, the extant literatures appear to exhibit a thickness limit for
observable skyrmions. The critical thickness limit for the formation of skyrmions may be based
on this FeTe /FGaT heterostructure strategy, as illustrated in Fig. 4. Fig. 4 investigates the
2
temperature dependence of Raman spectra in FGaT with varying thicknesses and threshold for the
precipitation of FeTe . Fig. 4a and 4b display the temperature-dependent Raman spectra for 15 nm
2
and 70 nm thick FGaT samples, respectively. At room temperature (303 K), both samples exhibit
a broad peak around 150 cm-1, characteristic of FGaT, confirming the presence of pure FGaT
before thermal annealing. As the temperature increases, the thicker sample (70 nm) begins to
precipitate FeTe evidenced by a weak signal of A mode (~120 cm-1) of FeTe emerging at 338 K.
2 g 2
By 368 K, the two characteristic FeTe peaks are clearly visible, indicating substantial precipitation.
2
In contrast, the thinner sample (15 nm) shows subtle signal of FeTe peaks only at 373 K, with
2
more pronounced features appearing only at 423 K (Fig. S22). The two samples, differing in
thickness, exhibit a notable disparity in the temperature at which FeTe
2
precipitation occurs.

To further explore the role of thickness and temperature on FeTe precipitation, Raman
2
spectra were collected for samples with thicknesses ranging from 15 to 600 nm. As shown in Fig.
4c, FeTe precipitation exhibits a strong dependence on sample thickness. The transition
2
temperature was defined as the point at which the intensity ratio of FeTe to FGaT Raman peaks
2
exceeds 1/3 (Fig. S22), indicating a certain amount of FeTe precipitation at this temperature. This
2
approach ensures consistent quantification of FeTe
2
precipitation onset across thickness-dependent
datasets. The transition temperature reveals a distinct threshold at approximately 25 nm. For
samples thinner than 25 nm (red dots), the transition temperature ranges from 380–400 K, whereas
thicker samples (orange dots) precipitate FeTe at lower transition temperatures, between 320–350
2
K. This threshold indicates that thicker FGaT samples are more prone to FeTe
2
precipitation, with
a clear distinction in the transition temperatures based on the sample thickness. Furthermore, the
intensity ratio of FeTe to FGaT Raman peaks at the highest temperature (423 K) reinforces this
2
threshold. As shown in Fig. S22b, the ratios for thinner samples range from 1.5 to 2, while for
thicker samples, the ratios increase to 3.5 to 6. This suggests that thinner FGaT samples are less
likely to precipitate FeTe .
2
A comparison with the previous literatures (Fig. 4d) suggests that the observed thickness
threshold for FeTe precipitation closely aligns with the minimum thickness required for skyrmion
2
formation in FGaT, as reported earlier26,30. This further implies that FeTe precipitation plays a
2
critical role in skyrmion formation by providing the necessary symmetry breaking to stabilize
skyrmion lattices.

Optothermal creation of isolated single skyrmions via local phase engineering
The established link between FeTe precipitation and skyrmion stabilization was further
2
developed through the implementation of a laser annealing protocol on FGaT flake, thereby
facilitating the creation of site-specific skyrmions, which are crucial for spintronic applications.
As illustrated schematically in Fig. 5a, the FGaT sample was positioned under an out-of-plane
magnetic field with approximately 200 Oe, aligned with the FC condition. A 532 nm continuous-
wave laser was irradiated in a pre-designed 3×3 array pattern, generating localized thermal
annealing zones while maintaining an inter-spot distance of approximately 5 μm. The laser power
was set to 2.5 mW, which was optimized to be within the safe operating window for FeTe
2
precipitation (see Methods), and the irradiation time for each spot was five minutes. This duration
is sufficient to reach the temperature to induce FeTe precipitation, yet it remains well below the
2
threshold required to cause the degradation of the FGaT. This spatially selective laser annealing
process directly induced the formation of FeTe
2
nanodomains, as confirmed by Raman
spectroscopy. The Raman mapping of characteristic A
g
phonon mode at 121 cm-1 (Fig. 5b)
demonstrates exclusive intensity enhancement at all nine irradiated sites, while exhibiting no
detectable peak at this position in non-annealed regions. This site-specific spectral fingerprint
conclusively demonstrates FeTe
2
formation exclusively within laser-defined zones, with the
surrounding matrix retaining pristine FGaT characteristics. Notably, MFM image of these specific
locations revealed the presence of isolated single skyrmions, which exhibited precise positional
correspondence with the laser-defined sites. Fig. 5c shows a magnetic landscape divided by the
Raman mapping boundary (dashed box). Maze-like domains dominate the unmapped regions and
correspond to predominant ferromagnetic domains. In contrast, the scanned territory exhibits laser-
modified labyrinth-like domains, indicative of the reduced ferromagnetic phase42. Critically, only
the nine sites that were intentionally irradiated and coincided with Raman mapping hotspots
nucleated isolated single skyrmions (with diameters of 300-400 nm) that were confined to laser-
spot dimensions, demonstrating phase-specific magnetic engineering by laser control. These laser-
patterned single-skyrmion arrays enable a room-temperature operation without FC process. Their
deterministic positioning and ambient operational stability overcome persistent scalability barriers
in topological computing architectures. This breakthrough paves the way for implementing energy-
efficient spintronic logic gates with nanoscale resolution, enabling next-generation spintronic
memory and logic devices29,46. Fig. 5d demonstrates a skyrmion-based AND logic gate enabled by
our laser-directed single-skyrmion writing technique, which provides the critical foundation for
programmable topological computing. By leveraging deterministic laser patterning (Fig. 5a-c), we
successfully created individual single-skyrmion in FGaT by laser FC. Binary inputs are encoded
via single-skyrmions core polarization (up/down) defined as logic states “0” for up and “1” for
down with the polarization direction set by external magnetic field orientation during laser FC. As
illustrated in Fig. 5d, the two input skyrmions are created at the top- and bottom-right corners. A
pulse current is utilized to concurrently drive the skyrmions towards the center47,48. Input pairs
aligned in parallel (0–0 or 1–1) undergo coherent merging, preserving the topological
configuration. In contrast, antiparallel input combinations (0–1 or 1–0) result in topological
annihilation, collapsing into a trivial ferromagnetic state. The output is detected via a tunneling
magnetoresistance (TMR) sensor, which registers a logical '1' only detecting a surviving down-
polarized skyrmion. This mechanism enables Boolean AND functionality with zero static power
consumption, showcasing the feasibility of energy-efficient, reconfigurable topological logic
operations.

## Methods

Fe
3
GaTe
2
single crystal growth
FGaTcrystals were grown using the self-flux method. Highly pure Fe (99.9 %), Ga (99.99 %),
and Te (99.99 %) powders, with a mole ratio of 1:1:2, were mixed under Ar atmosphere in a glove box
and sealed in a quartz tube under 1.9 Pa. To capture the excess flux during centrifugation, a crucible
filled with quartz wool was placed on top of the growth crucible. The melt was homogenized at 1000 °C
for approximately 24 hours, then cooled quickly to 880 °C in 1 hour, followed by slow cooling to
780 °C in 100 hours. At this temperature, the ampoules were removed from the furnace and placed in
a centrifuge to expel the excess flux. Then large single crystals could be obtained. FGaTnanoflakes
were mechanically exfoliated onto a freshly cleaned SiO2/Si substrate
. In our experiment, the pristine
FGaT nanoflakes were mechanically exfoliated onto a freshly cleaned SiO2/Si substrate with the
thicknesses ranging from 12 to 600 nm (Fig. S1).

Magnetic force microscopy measurements
MFM measurements on FGaT were performed using the DIMENSION ICON (Bruker). The
magnetic field during FC was generated by a neodymium magnet. The measurement was conducted in
a glove box protected by high-purity nitrogen gas at room temperature. The magnetic tip from
Nanoworld coated with Co/Cr was used for all measurements. The force constant and resonance
frequency of this tip are 3 N/m and 75 kHz, respectively. During the measurement, the topography of
the sample was first acquired in tapping mode. During the second scan, the MFM tip was lifted by 100
nm above the sample to measure the magnetic signal in tapping mode. MFM measurements on FGeT
were carried out using variable temperature MFM system (attocube-2100). Hard magnetic point probes
with cobalt coating (Nanosensors) were employed. The samples were cooled from room temperature
to 150 K in a low-pressure helium gas environment under zero magnetic field. Prior to MFM imaging,
a relatively flat region was identified using tapping mode AFM, and slope compensation was
performed to ensure a constant tip-sample distance across the scan area. Phase images were then
acquired at a fixed tip-sample separation, typically set to 100 nm.

Raman Spectroscopy measurements
The Raman measurements were obtained by a Witec Alpha 300R confocal Raman microscope.
The 532 nm linear polarized laser was focused perpendicular to the surface of the sample through a
100x objective lens (numerical aperture = 0.9). The maximum power is kept below 0.2 mW to avoid
the laser thermal effects on the sample. The Raman signals were first collected by a photonic crystal
fiber and then coupled into the spectrometer with 1800 g/mm grating.

HAADF-STEM
STEM specimens were prepared by the focused ion beam (FIB) lift-out technique using the FEI
Helios 5cx system. Atomic resolution STEM images were performed on an aberration-corrected FEI
Themis Z transmission electron microscopy, equipped with a cold field-emission gun operating at 200
kV. The resolution ADF-STEM images were collected with a convergence semiangle of 24.5 mrad,
collecting scattering from >44 mrad. Image filtered using Gaussian functions.

Theoretical calculation
The relaxed crystal structures were obtained using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package
(VASP) within the framework of density functional theory (DFT). The exchange-correlation
functional was described using the general gradient approximation (GGA) as parameterized
by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE). The plane -wave energy cutoff and convergence threshold
were set to 450 eV and 10- 6 eV, respectively. Phonon spectra with a 2×2×2 supercell were
calculated using the finite-displacement method implemented in the Phonopy code.

Micromagnetic simulation
Micromagnetic simulation was carried out with MuMax3 software based on the Landu–
Lifshitz–Gilbert equation. Slab geometries of dimensions 10.2 μm × 10.2 μm × 300 nm were used
for the simulations of magnetic field-driven spin textures evolutions and the generation of zero-
field skyrmions. The following parameters were used in the simulations: saturation magnetization
M = 3 × 105 A/m, Ku = 9 × 104 J/m3, the exchange constant A = 8 × 10−12 A/m, the DMI coefficient
D = 0.1 mJ/m2 for pristine FGaT and 2.0 mJ/m2 for FeTe /FGaT interface, and the damping constant
2
𝛼 = 0.2. An out-of-plane magnetic field of 300 Oe was applied during the FC procedure.

Laser patterning and localized phase engineering
For the deterministic creation of isolated skyrmions via optothermal writing, a continuous‑wave
laser (532 nm) was focused through a 100x objective lens (NA=0.9) onto the surface of the FGaT
flake (thickness > 25 nm). The laser power was set to 2.5 mW, selected within the determined
operating window of 0.5–4 mW (bounded by the phase transition threshold and ablation limit),
and the exposure time for each irradiation spot was fixed at 5 minutes. A pre‑designed 3 × 3 array
pattern was written with an inter‑spot distance of approximately 5 μm. During irradiation, the
sample was held under an out‑of‑plane magnetic field of about 200 Oe. The same optical path was
used for subsequent confocal Raman verification, with the laser power reduced below 0.2 mW to
avoid additional thermal modification during mapping.

The article describes the origin and applications of skyrmions in the 2D ferromagnetic material Fe3GaTe2 at room temperature. The authors demonstrated a spontaneous formation of FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface during field cooling, which had been overlooked in previous studies. This interface enhances the DMI which is crucial for skyrmion formation and resolves a longstanding issue of the DMI origin in Fe3GaTe2. They further demonstrated the precise generation of single skyrmions via laser-based field cooling. I believe this paper holds significant novelty and importance in both experimental mechanisms and application potential, making it worthy of publication in Nature Communications. However, there are some minor concerns.
1. The experimental evidence linking the FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface to skyrmions formation is convincing, while the theoretical explain seems a bit sparse. Can you explain more how the FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface affect the DMI enhancement?
2. SHG is important for studying symmetry. Have you tested angle-resolved polarized SHG? What should the polarization of the FeTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface be?
3. The article mentions the universality of FeTe2 precipitation, which might be crucial for surface structures and physics besides DMI and skyrmions. Does this phenomenon occur in other ternary tellurides?
4. The localized single skyrmions are groundbreaking. The device concept is also intriguing and promising. However, some important articles in this field have not been cited, such as (1) Nature Nanotechnology 16, 1086-1091 (2021) (2) Nature Nanotechnology 12, 123-126 (2017).

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Xia .et.al. deals with the determination of different phases during the annealing process of Fe3GaTe2 and Fe3GeTe2 crystals and its impact on the formation of magnetic textures. The authors provide an extensive characterization to support their claims. While the data clearly points to the formation of a secondary phase (FeTe2) that precipitates in a crystalline way towards the surface, the mechanism of skyrmion formation and claimed “enhancement of DMI interaction” is not well described and understood. In particular, the occurrence of symmetry breaking and induced skyrmion-like magnetic textures can have various origins besides the claimed FGaT/FeTe2 interface , such as self-intercalation, point defects, other magnetic phases, etc. Especially in systems that undergo precipitation, a plethora of changes may occur to the initial crystal phase. It is now well known in the community that TEM data (in which the authors base) is extremely local for a crystal that is macroscopic and not necessarily representative of the sample behaviour. Additional large-scale techniques to rule out the presence of point defects (e.g. Te-deficiency) and self-intercalation of surplus Fe -which can migrate not only to the top, but also to the bottom FGaT layer,- should be employed: for instance X-ray diffraction to resolve the FGaT structure before and after annealing (akin Phys. Rev. Materials 4, 074008 (2020) and Physical Review Letters 133 (25), 256702 (2024)). Additionally, the authors should discuss the influence of second Fe-Ga precipitate phase on the magnetic properties, in particular on the effect on MFM imaging as this phase is concentrated at the surface. This is necessary to unveil the origin of the observed SHG response and skyrmion-like bubble formation which is one of the most important aspects of the paper. The authors should address this main issue in a revised manuscript, as well as several other points:
1) The Raman-signal in Figure 1 show a full transition from one phase to another, without overlap of the two phases (as it was detected by TEM, Figure 2). The authors should comment if the surface sensitivity of their Raman setup is in line with the observation of only the FeTe2 phase after annealing.
2) SHG measurements. If the creation of a non-centrosymmetric structure happens only at the interface, it might reflect on a very weak signal. However, if it comes from a rather bulk phenomenon, it should scale with thickness. The authors should perform thickness dependent SHG measurements (samples shown in Figure 4c) to corroborate the origin of the signal.
3) There is another surface layer which consists of Fe-Ga rich amorphous phase. What is the thickness and influence of this layer on the various measurements? Since it contains Fe, it is probably magnetic. Could you provide magnetization measurements of the crystals before and after annealing? Is this also possible affecting magnetic bubble formation? MFM is surface sensitive so it will actually get stronger signals from the topmost layer.
4) How do you get the DMI constant of the FeTe2/FGaT interface as D = 2.0 mJ/m2? Can you provide calculation/estimation details?
5) The title states: “enhancement of DMI”, but there is no direct experimental evidence of DMI enhancement. The magnetic bubble formation is a hint that DMI might be the reason behind, but is very qualitative and does not merit the claim in the title. Even though, it is not clear whether it is a bulk or an interface-driven DMI. Either the authors bring more quantitative evidence or they should tone down the DMI statements in the manuscript.
6) In the laser-patterning experiment, is it possible to control laser parameters and define the boundaries of FeTe2 formation, similar to the heating study? That would serve as a practical guide for other scientists that may want to reproduce the results.
7) “The bond-free vdW interfaces in FeTe2/FGaT enable seamless integration of dissimilar materials without lattice-matching constraints, preserving spin coherence for low-1 power spintronic devices.” This sentence is misleading. The preservation of spin coherence is not automatically given at a vdW interface of dissimilar materials.

## Abstract

Room-temperature skyrmions in the two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnet
Fe GaTe (FGaT) hold great promise for spintronics. However, the origin of the necessary
3 2
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) within its centrosymmetric lattice remains elusive. Here,

3 2

## Introduction

Since long-range magnetic orders were realized in atomically thin materials, including
ferromagnetism (FM, e.g., CrI and Cr Ge Te 1,2) and antiferromagnetism (AFM, e.g., FePS 3,4),
3 2 2 6 3
more and more two-dimensional (2D) magnets are being investigated by thinning down van der
Waals (vdW) magnetic materials. Plenty of new magnetic properties emerge at the 2D limit, such
as layer-dependent magnetism1,5-7, strong magnetic anisotropy2,8-10, quantum anomalous Hall
effect (QAHE)11,12 and nonlinear topological magnetic structures13-15, offering unprecedented
opportunities for miniaturized spintronic devices. Among these emerging phenomena, magnetic
skyrmions—topologically protected spin textures—have garnered intense interest due to their
potential as information carriers in ultrahigh-density memory and logic architectures15-17.

The formation and stabilization of skyrmions are strongly related to the Dzyaloshinskii-
Moriya interaction (DMI), which arises from broken inversion symmetry and induces chiral spin
textures18-20. Over an extended duration, a proper DMI for generation of skyrmions relies on
growth of chiral magnetic materials14,21 or fabrication of delicately designed heterostructures with
alternative ferromagnetic and heavy-metal films16,22, where cryogenic temperature is still
necessary for the realization of skyrmions23-25.

Recently, room-temperature skyrmions and skyrmion lattice are generated in 2D
ferromagnetic material Fe GaTe (FGaT), whose Curie transition temperature (T ) is around 350-
3 2 C
380 K, by simple field cooling (FC) at moderate temperature26-33. Such breakthrough observations
herald a transformative era in the development of vdW magnets and topological magnetic orders.
However, there persists a fundamental paradox regarding the formation of skyrmions in FGaT:
where does the DMI stem from in such a centrosymmetric crystal structure (P6 /mmc). Recent
3
studies have proposed diverse origins for DMI in FGaT, including Fe vacancies30, atomic
displacement28,29, surface oxidization34,35 and intercalation of Fe atoms32. While these studies
propose miscellaneous hypotheses regarding the origin of DMI, a unified understanding of the
dominant mechanism has yet to emerge.

Apart from the above observations, an unavoidable fact has been largely neglected. To
generate skyrmions in FGaT, thermal treatment during the FC on the sample is unavoidable, and
tellurides, especially ternary compounds, are prone to phase transitions or surface
reconstruction36,37. Therefore, in this study, we investigate the influence of the FC on DMI and
skyrmion formation in FGaTand Fe GeTe (FGeT), revealing the mechanisms of the emergent
3 2

transmission electron microscopy (STEM), we reveal that the commonly used FC process causes
the irreversible precipitation of FeTe thin layers at the surfaces of the annealed FGaT. The resulted

## Methods

Fe
3
GaTe
2
single crystal growth
FGaTcrystals were grown using the self-flux method. Highly pure Fe (99.9 %), Ga (99.99 %),
and Te (99.99 %) powders, with a mole ratio of 1:1:2, were mixed under Ar atmosphere in a glove box
and sealed in a quartz tube under 1.9 Pa. To capture the excess flux during centrifugation, a crucible
filled with quartz wool was placed on top of the growth crucible. The melt was homogenized at 1000 °C
for approximately 24 hours, then cooled quickly to 880 °C in 1 hour, followed by slow cooling to
780 °C in 100 hours. At this temperature, the ampoules were removed from the furnace and placed in
a centrifuge to expel the excess flux. Then large single crystals could be obtained. FGaTnanoflakes
were mechanically exfoliated onto a freshly cleaned SiO2/Si substrate
. In our experiment, the pristine
FGaT nanoflakes were mechanically exfoliated onto a freshly cleaned SiO2/Si substrate with the
thicknesses ranging from 12 to 600 nm (Fig. S1).

Magnetic force microscopy measurements
MFM measurements on FGaT were performed using the DIMENSION ICON (Bruker). The
magnetic field during FC was generated by a neodymium magnet. The measurement was conducted in
a glove box protected by high-purity nitrogen gas at room temperature. The magnetic tip from
Nanoworld coated with Co/Cr was used for all measurements. The force constant and resonance
frequency of this tip are 3 N/m and 75 kHz, respectively. During the measurement, the topography of
the sample was first acquired in tapping mode. During the second scan, the MFM tip was lifted by 100
nm above the sample to measure the magnetic signal in tapping mode. MFM measurements on FGeT
were carried out using variable temperature MFM system (attocube-2100). Hard magnetic point probes
with cobalt coating (Nanosensors) were employed. The samples were cooled from room temperature
to 150 K in a low-pressure helium gas environment under zero magnetic field. Prior to MFM imaging,
a relatively flat region was identified using tapping mode AFM, and slope compensation was
performed to ensure a constant tip-sample distance across the scan area. Phase images were then
acquired at a fixed tip-sample separation, typically set to 100 nm.

Raman Spectroscopy measurements
The Raman measurements were obtained by a Witec Alpha 300R confocal Raman microscope.
The 532 nm linear polarized laser was focused perpendicular to the surface of the sample through a
100x objective lens (numerical aperture = 0.9). The maximum power is kept below 0.2 mW to avoid
the laser thermal effects on the sample. The Raman signals were first collected by a photonic crystal
fiber and then coupled into the spectrometer with 1800 g/mm grating.

HAADF-STEM
STEM specimens were prepared by the focused ion beam (FIB) lift-out technique using the FEI
Helios 5cx system. Atomic resolution STEM images were performed on an aberration-corrected FEI
Themis Z transmission electron microscopy, equipped with a cold field-emission gun operating at 200
kV. The resolution ADF-STEM images were collected with a convergence semiangle of 24.5 mrad,
collecting scattering from >44 mrad. Image filtered using Gaussian functions.

Theoretical calculation
The relaxed crystal structures were obtained using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package
(VASP) within the framework of density functional theory (DFT). The exchange-correlation
functional was described using the general gradient approximation (GGA) as parameterized
by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE). The plane -wave energy cutoff and convergence threshold
were set to 450 eV and 10- 6 eV, respectively. Phonon spectra with a 2×2×2 supercell were
calculated using the finite-displacement method implemented in the Phonopy code.

Micromagnetic simulation
Micromagnetic simulation was carried out with MuMax3 software based on the Landu–
Lifshitz–Gilbert equation. Slab geometries of dimensions 10.2 μm × 10.2 μm × 300 nm were used
for the simulations of magnetic field-driven spin textures evolutions and the generation of zero-
field skyrmions. The following parameters were used in the simulations: saturation magnetization
M = 3 × 105 A/m, Ku = 9 × 104 J/m3, the exchange constant A = 8 × 10−12 A/m, the DMI coefficient
D = 0.1 mJ/m2 for pristine FGaT and 2.0 mJ/m2 for FeTe /FGaT interface, and the damping constant
2
𝛼 = 0.2. An out-of-plane magnetic field of 300 Oe was applied during the FC procedure.

Laser patterning and localized phase engineering
For the deterministic creation of isolated skyrmions via optothermal writing, a continuous‑wave
laser (532 nm) was focused through a 100x objective lens (NA=0.9) onto the surface of the FGaT
flake (thickness > 25 nm). The laser power was set to 2.5 mW, selected within the determined
operating window of 0.5–4 mW (bounded by the phase transition threshold and ablation limit),
and the exposure time for each irradiation spot was fixed at 5 minutes. A pre‑designed 3 × 3 array
pattern was written with an inter‑spot distance of approximately 5 μm. During irradiation, the
